title: 10 Vietnamese Foods You Must Try
excerpt: A traveler's shortlist of iconic dishes across the North, Central, and South.
author: Vietnam Food Guide
content: Vietnamese cuisine is regional, seasonal, and deeply tied to place. Start with pho in Hanoi, bun bo Hue in the Center, and banh mi in the South.
Use this list as a flexible itinerary: try one signature dish per city, then explore local specialties once you know your flavor preferences.
Remember that street stalls often serve the most memorable versions — follow the crowd and look for busy kitchens.

title: Vietnamese Coffee Culture
excerpt: From ca phe sua da to egg coffee — how Vietnam drinks coffee.
author: Vietnam Food Guide
content: Vietnamese coffee is typically robusta-based, strong, and sweetened with condensed milk.
In Hanoi, egg coffee turns the daily coffee ritual into dessert. In the South, iced milk coffee is a street-side essential.
Take time to sit, watch the street, and enjoy the slow drip — coffee here is as much about pace as caffeine.

title: Northern vs Central vs Southern Cuisine
excerpt: How flavor, ingredients, and cooking styles shift from Hanoi to Hue to Saigon.
author: Vietnam Food Guide
content: The North prefers subtle, balanced seasoning. The Center embraces chili and complexity. The South leans sweeter and more tropical.
Understanding these differences helps travelers choose dishes that match their taste — and appreciate why the same noodle soup can taste completely different by region.

title: Vietnamese Street Food Guide
excerpt: Practical tips for eating well, safely, and locally on the street.
author: Vietnam Food Guide
content: Look for busy stalls with high turnover. Bring small cash. Learn a few food words.
Start with cooked dishes if you are new to street food, then explore fresh rolls and salads once you feel comfortable.

title: What to Eat in Hanoi?
excerpt: A one-day and three-day food plan for Vietnam's capital.
author: Vietnam Food Guide
content: Begin with pho or bun cha for lunch, egg coffee in the afternoon, and a walk through the Old Quarter for evening snacks.
Hanoi rewards curiosity — ask locals for their favorite neighborhood spots beyond the famous tourist addresses.

title: What to Eat in Hue?
excerpt: Royal flavors, spicy noodles, and humble clam rice in the former imperial city.
author: Vietnam Food Guide
content: Hue cuisine is bold and spicy. Bun bo Hue is essential, but do not miss com hen and the city's many small royal-inspired dishes.
Portions can be small and refined — perfect for sampling many flavors in one meal.

title: Vietnamese Food Etiquette
excerpt: Simple manners that help travelers dine respectfully.
author: Vietnam Food Guide
content: Wait for elders to begin when dining with locals. Use serving chopsticks or utensils for shared dishes when provided.
It is polite to try a little of everything and to thank the host. Street dining is casual — still, keep queues orderly and tables tidy.
